title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident shows a deliberate attempt to manipulate AI retrieval and citation systems by flooding the web with fabricated authoritative content. A fictitious institution with no legal standing, no address, and no named personnel produced a very large volume of quasi-academic text in a short time, formatted specifically to match the query patterns that chatbots use when sourcing answers. The failure mode is not a malfunction inside any AI system but a vulnerability in how those systems treat surface credibility, volume, and formatting as proxies for reliability.

The exploitation point is upstream of the AI, sitting in the data environment the systems draw on. Catching it would have required either pre-publication vetting of sources used for retrieval-augmented generation, or anomaly detection capable of flagging an institution that produced more than half a million words in nine days while leaving no verifiable institutional trace. Neither capability is standard in deployed consumer AI systems.

What is not established is whether any named AI system actually cited the Hanover Institute's content, or whether the operation succeeded in shifting AI-generated outputs in the intended direction. The reporting describes intent and infrastructure, not confirmed effect.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
# Summary

A fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute, funded by the Israeli government, published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days to influence artificial intelligence chatbots toward pro-Israel arguments. The institute has no legal existence, physical address, or named staff, and its website presents Israeli government positions on topics like Palestinian torture and Gaza casualties in a quasi-academic format designed to appear neutral. The operation used a specialized platform optimized to get AI systems to cite the content, with questions formatted to match typical chatbot search queries.

The campaign is part of a much larger effort financed by tens of millions of dollars from Israel's government and routed through the European advertising company Havas Media and American contractors including Brad Parscale's Clock Tower X. Israeli officials have expressed frustration that these public diplomacy efforts have failed, with one comparing the spending to a major intelligence scandal. Meanwhile, American public opinion has shifted significantly against Israel, with polls showing growing sympathy for Palestinians and concerns about Israeli military actions in Gaza, particularly among younger voters.
